questions.title: Component not part of cell-membrane molecular structure
questions.question: Molecular structure of cell membrane include the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The phospholipid bilayer is the structural backbone of the plasma membrane, so it is a true membrane component, not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. Ribophorins are receptor proteins on the outer, cytoplasmic surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum that bind the large ribosomal subunit; they are a rough-ER feature, not a component of the plasma membrane's own molecular structure. Confusing the two is easy because both are membranous organelles studded with functional proteins, but the plasma membrane's protein components are peripheral and integral proteins, not ribophorins. This is the deliberately placed distractor testing whether the student can separate plasma-membrane composition from rough-ER composition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholesterol lies among the phospholipid fatty-acid tails and stabilises the membrane, so it is a genuine structural component.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Integral (transmembrane) proteins are one of the two protein classes built into the membrane, so they are a true component.

questions.learning_objective: Name the true molecular components of the plasma membrane and distinguish ribophorins as a rough-ER, not a membrane, feature.

questions.title: Meaning of "unit membrane"
questions.question: Unit membrane means:

options.C: One electron dense line with its associated cell coat.
options.D: Cell boundaries as seen by L.M.

explanations.A: Correct. "Unit membrane" is the electron-microscopic term for the plasma membrane's trilaminar appearance: two electron-dense lines (the polar phospholipid heads and associated protein) separated by an electron-lucent middle line (the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails). This trilaminar image is only resolved by electron microscopy, at roughly 7.5-10 nm thickness, and is the structural basis for calling every cell's surface membrane a "unit" of the same basic three-layered design. It is not visible with the light microscope and is not demonstrated by any light-microscopic stain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A phospholipid layer is only one component of the membrane, not the term for its overall trilaminar EM appearance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes a single dense line, not the three-layered (trilaminar) unit-membrane image.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cell boundaries are not resolved as a distinct structure by light microscopy at all; the unit membrane is an electron-microscopic finding.

questions.learning_objective: Define the unit membrane as the plasma membrane's trilaminar electron-microscopic appearance.

questions.title: Cholesterol in the cell membrane
questions.question: About Cholesterol molecules in cell membrane all true except:

options.B: Present in the inner & outer phospholipid layers.
options.C: Its function is stabilization of the cell membrane.
options.D: Keep the phospholipid molecules packed together.

explanations.A: Correct. The cell coat (glycocalyx) is a carbohydrate layer of glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer membrane surface only; cholesterol is a lipid that sits among the phospholipid fatty-acid tails within the bilayer itself, not in the carbohydrate coat external to it. Placing cholesterol in the cell coat mixes up two separate membrane-associated structures with different compositions and locations. This is the false statement the question is testing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: cholesterol is distributed in both the inner and the outer phospholipid leaflets, not restricted to one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: cholesterol's principal role is to stabilise the membrane by restricting excessive phospholipid movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: by wedging between fatty-acid tails, cholesterol keeps the phospholipid molecules more closely and uniformly packed.

questions.learning_objective: State where cholesterol sits in the plasma membrane and that it is not a cell-coat component.

questions.title: Function not carried out by the cell coat
questions.question: The following are functions of cell coat except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cell adhesion is a true cell-coat function: its glycoprotein/glycolipid molecules mediate cell-to-cell and cell-to-matrix attachment.
explanations.B: Correct. Carbohydrate metabolism is a biochemical process carried out inside the cytoplasm, not a function of the cell coat. The cell coat is itself built of carbohydrate (glycoproteins and glycolipids) and does the cell's recognising, adhering and receiving, but it does not metabolise carbohydrate; that role belongs to cytosolic and mitochondrial enzyme pathways such as glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. This is the deliberately placed "sounds related but is not" distractor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Receptor formation is a true cell-coat function: it carries the cell's specific receptors for hormones, drugs, bacteria and viruses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cell recognition is a true cell-coat function: its surface molecules, including blood-group antigens, let one cell identify another.

questions.learning_objective: List the true functions of the cell coat (adhesion, recognition, receptor formation) and exclude carbohydrate metabolism.

questions.title: Statement not true of the cell membrane
questions.question: About cell membrane, the following is true except:

options.A: Appears as Trilaminar appearance by E.M.
options.C: Seen by L.M. in all cells.
options.D: Its outer & inner layers include different types of phospholipids & proteins.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the trilaminar appearance by electron microscopy is the defining feature of the unit membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: 7.5-10 nm is the accepted thickness range for the plasma membrane.
explanations.C: Correct. The plasma membrane is not resolved as a distinct structure by the light microscope in any cell; it requires electron microscopy for direct visualisation, or a special stain such as silver or PAS acting on its outer carbohydrate coat to be inferred by light microscopy. Claiming it is "seen by LM in all cells" contradicts the basic reason the unit membrane is defined as an electron-microscopic finding in the first place. This is the false statement being tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: the membrane is asymmetric, with different phospholipid and protein compositions on its outer and inner leaflets.

questions.learning_objective: State that the plasma membrane is not resolved by light microscopy and requires EM (or special staining of its coat) to be demonstrated.

questions.title: Statement not true of membrane proteins
questions.question: About membrane proteins, the following is true except:

options.A: Has 2 main types, integral & peripheral membrane proteins.
options.B: Proteins are a major molecular constituent of the cell membrane (about 50%) [according to weight].
options.C: Peripheral membrane proteins are embedded within the lipids bilayer.
options.D: Peripheral membrane protein function as support for the cytoskeleton.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: integral and peripheral proteins are the two recognised classes of membrane protein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: protein makes up roughly half the membrane's mass.
explanations.C: Correct. Peripheral proteins are loosely attached to either the inner or outer membrane surface; they are not embedded within the lipid bilayer at all. Being embedded within (crossing) the bilayer is the defining feature of integral (transmembrane) proteins, so this statement swaps the two protein classes. This is the classic integral-versus-peripheral trap this MCQ bank returns to repeatedly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: on the inner surface, peripheral proteins form the cytoskeletal attachment layer that supports the membrane.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish integral (embedded, transmembrane) from peripheral (loosely surface-attached) membrane proteins.

questions.title: True statement about integral membrane proteins
questions.question: Integral membrane proteins:

options.A: Are loosely attached to the outer part of phospholipid bilayer.
options.B: Are not attached to the inner part of phospholipid bilayer.
options.C: Are the main cause for stability of the membrane.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Loose attachment describes peripheral, not integral, proteins; integral proteins cross the bilayer rather than sitting loosely on it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Integral (transmembrane) proteins span the bilayer and so are attached to, and pass through, both the inner and outer parts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholesterol, not integral protein, is the principal stabiliser of membrane fluidity; integral proteins carry out transport and signalling roles instead.
explanations.D: Correct. Because an integral protein spans the full thickness of the bilayer, it can form a continuous pore or channel across the membrane, allowing ions and small polar molecules such as water to cross; this channel-forming role, together with acting as a carrier or pump, is one of the defining functions of integral membrane proteins. A peripheral protein, confined to one surface, cannot form a transmembrane channel. This is why channel-protein function is used to identify the integral class specifically.

questions.learning_objective: State that only integral membrane proteins, which span the bilayer, can act as channel proteins.

questions.title: Statement not true of intrinsic (integral) membrane proteins
questions.question: Intrinsic or integral membrane proteins, all true except:

options.B: May act as ion channels or ion pumps
options.C: Each molecule has a non-polar hydrophobic region and a polar hydrophilic region.
options.D: Present in the Inner lipid layer only

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: integral proteins commonly act as receptors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: integral proteins act as ion channels and ion pumps (for example the sodium-potassium pump).
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: an integral protein has both a hydrophobic transmembrane region and hydrophilic regions facing the aqueous environment on each side.
explanations.D: Correct. Integral proteins are transmembrane: they cross both the inner and the outer lipid layers, not the inner layer alone. Restricting them to the inner layer only contradicts the defining feature of the integral class, which is that it spans the entire bilayer. This is the false statement being tested.

questions.learning_objective: State that integral proteins span both lipid layers rather than being confined to one.

questions.title: Statement not true of integral protein
questions.question: The following statements are true about integral protein EXCEPT:

options.A: Each molecule has hydrophilic & hydrophobic region.
options.C: It is loosely bound to the surface of lipid bilayer.
options.D: It may extend from one side of the cell membrane to the other side

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: an integral protein has both a hydrophobic (embedded) and a hydrophilic (surface-facing) region.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: integral proteins form channels and act as carriers for ions and small polar molecules.
explanations.C: Correct. "Loosely bound to the surface" describes a peripheral protein, not an integral one. An integral protein is firmly embedded within, and typically spans, the lipid bilayer; it is not resting loosely on a surface the way a peripheral protein does. This is the integral-versus-peripheral swap this bank repeatedly tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: an integral (transmembrane) protein can extend from one side of the membrane to the other.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This is true: an integral protein is tightly, not loosely, associated with the phospholipid bilayer it is embedded in.

questions.learning_objective: State that an integral protein is tightly embedded in (not loosely bound to the surface of) the lipid bilayer.

questions.title: Statement not true of extrinsic (peripheral) proteins
questions.question: Extrinsic or peripheral membrane proteins, all true except:

options.A: These are loosely bound to both inner and outer surfaces of the cell membrane
options.B: Its surface lacks the non-polar portion

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: peripheral proteins are loosely attached to either the inner or the outer membrane surface.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: peripheral proteins are entirely hydrophilic and lack the non-polar (hydrophobic) portion needed to embed in the bilayer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: on the inner surface, peripheral proteins anchor and support the cytoskeleton.
explanations.D: Correct. Acting as a receptor is a role of integral, transmembrane proteins, which can bind an extracellular ligand and transmit the signal across the membrane; a peripheral protein, being confined to one surface with no transmembrane segment, does not perform this receptor role. This is the integral-versus-peripheral function swap being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that acting as a receptor is an integral-, not peripheral-, protein function.

questions.title: True statement about integral membrane proteins
questions.question: Integral membrane proteins are;

options.A: not attached to the outer leaflets.
options.B: Main function in the stability of the membrane.
options.D: not attached to the inner leaflets

explanations.A: Incorrect. Integral proteins are attached to, and typically cross, the outer leaflet, not excluded from it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Membrane stability is chiefly cholesterol's role; integral proteins' main functions are transport, channel and receptor roles.
explanations.C: Correct. Transmembrane proteins, which span the full thickness of the bilayer from one surface to the other, are the classic and most familiar subtype of integral protein; the term "integral" is used specifically because these proteins are built into (integral to) the membrane structure rather than resting on it. This makes "includes transmembrane proteins" a direct, true description of the integral class.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Integral proteins are attached to, and typically cross, the inner leaflet as well, not excluded from it.

questions.learning_objective: State that transmembrane proteins are a subtype of integral membrane protein.

questions.title: Function not carried out by the plasma membrane
questions.question: The plasma membrane has the following functions EXCEPT;

options.B: It is the primary site of protein biosynthesis
options.C: It is a cell adhesion interface
options.D: It is a site for hormone receptors.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Selective permeability, controlling what enters and leaves the cell, is a core membrane function.
explanations.B: Correct. Protein biosynthesis is carried out by ribosomes, both free in the cytosol and attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, not by the plasma membrane. The plasma membrane's roles are barrier, adhesion, recognition and receptor functions; it has no ribosomes of its own and does not synthesise protein. This is the deliberately placed "wrong organelle" distractor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Via the cell coat and junctional proteins, the plasma membrane mediates adhesion between cells, so this is a true function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Integral proteins of the plasma membrane act as hormone receptors, so this is a true function.

questions.learning_objective: State that protein biosynthesis is a ribosome/rER function, not a plasma-membrane function.

questions.title: Statement not true of the cell coat (glycocalyx)
questions.question: About cell coat [glycocalyx], all true except:

options.A: Some of the outward-facing lipid molecules forming glycolipids.
options.B: Cholesterol is a main constituent of the cell coat.
options.C: Most of the outward-facing proteins constituting glycoproteins.
options.D: Has a key role in cell recognition and cell adhesion.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: outward-facing membrane lipids carry carbohydrate chains that form glycolipids, part of the coat.
explanations.B: Correct. The cell coat is built of carbohydrate attached to outward-facing lipid and protein molecules (glycolipids and glycoproteins); cholesterol is a lipid that lies within the bilayer itself and is not a constituent of the carbohydrate coat. This mixes the cell coat up with the membrane lipid bilayer beneath it, and is the false statement being tested.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: outward-facing membrane proteins similarly carry carbohydrate chains, forming glycoproteins, part of the coat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: cell recognition and adhesion are the cell coat's key roles.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cell coat is built of glycolipids and glycoproteins, not cholesterol.

questions.title: Statement not correct about the cell coat
questions.question: About cell coat, all of the following statements are correct EXCEPT;

options.B: it is located on the outer surface of the membrane.
options.D: it is involved in cell to cell recognition.

explanations.A: Correct. Cholesterol is a bilayer lipid, not a constituent of the carbohydrate-based cell coat; the coat is made of glycoproteins and glycolipids, not cholesterol. This is the same cholesterol-versus-cell-coat confusion tested in the previous question, restated here in a different item format.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: the cell coat lies on the outer surface of the membrane only.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: because it is carbohydrate, the cell coat stains positively with the periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: the cell coat mediates cell-to-cell recognition.

questions.learning_objective: State that cholesterol is not a cell-coat constituent, and that the coat is outer-surface, PAS-positive and recognition-related.

questions.title: Differences between the outer and inner aspects of the cell membrane
questions.question: Differences between the outer and inner aspects of the cell membrane, include the following except:

options.A: Cell coat & receptors are present on the outer surface only.
options.B: Different lipid components in both layers.
options.C: Different protein components in both layers.
options.D: Cholesterol is present in the outer layer only

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the cell coat and most receptors are outer-surface-only features, part of the membrane's asymmetry.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: the outer and inner phospholipid leaflets differ in the specific lipid species they carry.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: different proteins are also distributed asymmetrically between the two leaflets.
explanations.D: Correct. Cholesterol does not follow the outer-only pattern of the cell coat and most receptors; it is distributed among the fatty-acid tails of both the outer and the inner phospholipid layers, where it restricts phospholipid movement and stabilises the membrane on both sides. Extending the "outer surface only" rule from the cell coat/receptors to cholesterol is the error this question is built to catch.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish membrane features restricted to one leaflet (cell coat, receptors, specific lipids/proteins) from cholesterol, which is present in both.

questions.title: Method that does not demonstrate mitochondria by light microscopy
questions.question: Mitochondria can be demonstrated with L.M. by the following except:

options.B: Supravital staining with Janus Green B.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Silver impregnation is a recognised light-microscopic method for demonstrating mitochondria.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Supravital staining with Janus Green B is the classic method for demonstrating mitochondria in living cells, because the dye is selectively reduced by mitochondrial enzymes without killing the cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iron haematoxylin stains mitochondria dark blue/black and is a standard light-microscopic demonstration method.
explanations.D: Correct. Trypan blue is a vital dye used to test cell viability (it is excluded by living cells and taken up only by dead ones), not a mitochondrial stain; mitochondria are demonstrated with a supravital dye such as Janus Green B, which is a specifically different category of stain from a plain vital dye like trypan blue. Confusing "vital staining" in general with the specific supravital technique that actually marks mitochondria is the trap here.

questions.learning_objective: Name the light-microscopic methods (silver, iron haematoxylin, supravital Janus Green B) that demonstrate mitochondria, and exclude trypan blue.

questions.title: Content not found in the mitochondrial matrix
questions.question: Mitochondrial matrix contains the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the mitochondrial matrix holds the organelle's own DNA.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: the enzymes of fatty-acid beta-oxidation are located in the matrix.
explanations.C: Correct. The enzymes of oxidative phosphorylation are located on the inner mitochondrial membrane, specifically in the elementary particles studding the cristae, where the electron transport chain and ATP synthase actually work; they are not dissolved in the matrix. Placing phosphorylation enzymes in the matrix confuses the matrix (which holds the citric acid cycle, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes, DNA and calcium granules) with the inner membrane/cristae (which holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase). This location swap is the fact being tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: the citric acid (Krebs) cycle enzymes are located in the matrix.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish matrix contents (DNA, Krebs-cycle and fatty-acid-oxidation enzymes) from oxidative-phosphorylation enzymes, which sit on the cristae, not free in the matrix.

questions.title: Statement not true of mitochondria
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning mitochondria is true EXCEPT:

options.A: they contain enzymes for electron transport (respiration).

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the electron transport chain enzymes sit on the mitochondrial inner membrane/cristae.
explanations.B: Correct. Catalase is a defining marker enzyme of the peroxisome, where it breaks down the hydrogen peroxide generated by peroxisomal oxidases; it is not a mitochondrial enzyme. Assigning catalase to the mitochondrion confuses the two membranous, oxygen-handling organelles, which is exactly the distinction this question is built to test.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: the inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: the outer mitochondrial membrane is smooth, unlike the folded inner one.

questions.learning_objective: State that catalase is a peroxisomal, not a mitochondrial, marker enzyme.

questions.title: Statement not true of mitochondria
questions.question: All about mitochondria is true except:

options.D: Ca may be included in its matrix.

explanations.A: Correct. A mitochondrion is bounded by two separate unit membranes (an outer and an inner membrane), each itself a phospholipid bilayer, not simply "2 phospholipid layers" as a single flat description; describing the organelle this way understates its double-membrane architecture, with an intermembrane space between the two membranes and cristae folded from the inner one. This structural detail, rather than the membranes' lipid chemistry, is what the statement gets wrong.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: mitochondria are dynamic organelles that can change shape.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: mitochondria increase in number by simple division (fission) of pre-existing mitochondria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: dense, calcium-rich granules are a recognised matrix content.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the mitochondrion as bounded by two separate unit membranes rather than as a single generic phospholipid structure.

questions.title: Statement not true of mitochondria (second pass)
questions.question: All about mitochondria is true except:

options.A: Steroid forming cells contain mitochondria with tubular Cristae.
options.B: Can be seen by vital staining.
options.C: Can be demonstrated by phase contrast light microscopy.
options.D: Its life span is usually 10 days.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: tubular cristae are the recognised ultrastructural marker of a steroid-secreting cell's mitochondria.
explanations.B: Correct. Plain vital staining (a dye such as trypan blue that simply distinguishes living from dead cells) does not demonstrate mitochondria; mitochondria require the specific supravital technique, using a dye such as Janus Green B that living mitochondrial enzymes actively reduce, which is a distinct category from a generic vital stain. This same vital-versus-supravital distinction was tested directly in Q16 of this bank.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: phase-contrast light microscopy can show mitochondria (and their movement) in living, unstained cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: a mitochondrial lifespan of about ten days is the standard teaching figure.

questions.learning_objective: State that mitochondria require supravital (not plain vital) staining to be demonstrated by light microscopy.

questions.title: Function not carried out by mitochondria
questions.question: Mitochondria can do the following except:

options.A: Nucleic acids formation for its own use
options.C: Has role in Steroidogenesis in steroid forming cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: mitochondria contain their own DNA and synthesise the nucleic acids they need for their own replication.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: electron transport and ATP formation on the cristae are the mitochondrion's core function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: steroidogenic enzymes are located in mitochondria (and smooth ER) of steroid-secreting cells.
explanations.D: Correct. Detoxification of drugs is carried out by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which contains the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, not by mitochondria. Attaching detoxification to the mitochondrion instead of the sER is the deliberate cross-organelle confusion this question tests.

questions.learning_objective: State that drug detoxification is a smooth-ER, not a mitochondrial, function.

questions.title: Mitochondrial distribution in ion-transporting cells
questions.question: In ion transporting cells, mitochondria are present in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The apical surface faces the lumen and is not the site of the basal-infolding/mitochondria arrangement that powers ion transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral surface is where junctional complexes sit, not the vertically stacked mitochondria of the ion-pump region.
explanations.C: Correct. Ion-transporting epithelial cells (such as renal tubule and striated-duct cells) have deep basal plasma-membrane infoldings that increase the basal surface area; mitochondria are packed vertically between these infoldings to supply the large amount of ATP the basal sodium-potassium pumps need for active ion transport. This basal arrangement, matching structure to the site of highest metabolic demand, is the identifying feature the question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A perinuclear distribution is characteristic of cells with a single non-polar secretory face (such as neurons), not of polarised ion-transporting epithelial cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that mitochondria concentrate in the basal region of ion-transporting cells, packed between basal infoldings.

questions.title: Microscope used to detect mitochondrial movement in culture
questions.question: The type of microscope used to detect movement of the mitochondria in culture is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Scanning electron microscopy images fixed, metal-coated surfaces; it cannot show living, moving cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transmission electron microscopy needs fixed, ultra-thin sectioned, dead tissue; it gives a single static image, not real-time movement.
explanations.C: Correct. Phase-contrast microscopy converts small refractive-index differences within an unstained specimen into visible brightness differences, so it can image a living, unfixed, unstained cultured cell directly. Because no fixation or staining is needed, it is the technique used to watch real-time organelle movement, such as mitochondrial trafficking, inside a living cell over time.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ordinary (bright-field) light microscopy with a routine stain needs fixed, dead, coloured tissue and cannot show movement in a living, unstained cell.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Electric microscope" is not a recognised microscopy technique for this purpose.

questions.learning_objective: State that phase-contrast microscopy, not EM or routine light microscopy, is used to observe live organelle movement.

questions.title: True statements about mitochondria
questions.question: Mitochondria:

options.B: Cristae are carrying ATP synthetase which produce ATP.
options.C: In some cells Can generate heat.

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. This statement is true (mitochondria can move within the cytoplasm and divide by fission) but it is not the only true statement among the options.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. This statement is true (ATP synthase on the cristae generates ATP by oxidative phosphorylation) but it is not the only true statement among the options.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. This statement is true (brown-fat mitochondria use thermogenin to uncouple oxidation from ATP synthesis and generate heat instead) but it is not the only true statement among the options.
explanations.D: Correct. Mitochondria are motile and divide by fission, so they can move within the cytoplasm and increase their own numbers. Their cristae carry ATP synthase, the enzyme complex that makes ATP by oxidative phosphorylation, which is the organelle's central energy-producing role. In specialised cells such as brown adipose tissue, mitochondria instead generate heat rather than ATP, using thermogenin to uncouple the electron transport chain from ATP synthesis; because all three statements are independently true, "all the above" is the correct, most complete answer.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise mitochondrial motility/division, ATP synthase on the cristae, and thermogenic uncoupling as all true.

questions.title: Function not carried out by smooth ER
questions.question: The following are functions of sER except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: lipid and steroid metabolism are core sER functions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: drug and toxin detoxification (via cytochrome P450 enzymes) is a core sER function.
explanations.C: Correct. Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes, either free in the cytosol or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum; the smooth ER, by definition, lacks attached ribosomes and does not synthesise protein. This is the defining rough-versus-smooth ER distinction the question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: the sER regulates intracellular calcium, notably in muscle as the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.learning_objective: State that protein synthesis is a rough-, not smooth-, ER function.

questions.title: EM appearance of smooth endoplasmic reticulum
questions.question: By EM, smooth endoplasmic reticulum appears:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parallel flattened cisternae describe the rough, not the smooth, endoplasmic reticulum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dense-core vesicles describe secretory granules, not the tubular smooth ER network.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is the rough, not the smooth, ER whose outer membrane is continuous with the nuclear envelope's outer membrane.
explanations.D: Correct. By electron microscopy, the smooth endoplasmic reticulum appears as a network of branching and anastomosing (interconnecting) tubules, without the flattened, ribosome-studded, parallel-cisternae shape of the rough ER. This tubular, ribosome-free architecture is the structural feature that lets the smooth ER be identified on an electron micrograph.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Being prominent in protein-secreting cells describes the ribosome-rich rough ER, not the smooth ER, which is prominent instead in steroid-secreting and detoxifying cells.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the smooth ER's EM appearance as branching, anastomosing, ribosome-free tubules.

questions.title: Statement not true of steroid-forming cells
questions.question: Steroid forming cells are characterized by the following except:

options.D: Contain numerous mitochondria with tubular Cristae.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: steroid-forming cells are characteristically rich in smooth ER, which carries steroidogenic enzymes.
explanations.B: Correct. Steroid-forming cells are characterised by abundant smooth ER, not rough ER; they secrete a small lipid-soluble hormone directly, with no protein product to package, so they have comparatively little rough ER and few free ribosomes, and are typically acidophilic (not basophilic) on light microscopy as a result. Assigning rich rough ER to a steroid-forming cell reverses this defining ultrastructural pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: lipid droplets, the cholesterol precursor store for steroid synthesis, are abundant in these cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: tubular mitochondrial cristae are the classic ultrastructural marker of a steroidogenic cell.

questions.learning_objective: State that a steroid-forming cell's organelle profile is sER-rich, not rER-rich.

questions.title: Organelles a protein-secreting cell is rich in
questions.question: Protein secreting cells are rich in:

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. rER is true (it synthesises the exported protein) but it is not the only correct organelle among the options.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Golgi is true (it packages and modifies the protein for export) but it is not the only correct organelle among the options.
explanations.C: Correct. A protein-secreting cell needs an abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum to synthesise and segregate the protein it exports. It also needs an abundant Golgi apparatus to glycosylate, sort and package that protein into secretory vesicles. Because the two organelles work in direct sequence along the same secretory pathway, a cell rich in one is characteristically rich in the other as well, which is why both are correct together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both rER and Golgi are correct, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that a protein-secreting cell is rich in both rough ER and Golgi apparatus.

questions.title: Statement not true of rough endoplasmic reticulum
questions.question: About rER all is true except:

options.A: connected with the smooth ER and the outer nuclear membrane.
options.B: Interconnected flattened parallel cisternae studded with ribosomes
options.C: Result in diffuse basophilia seen with L.M.
options.D: proteins are transferred to the Golgi apparatus via the transfer vesicles

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: rER is continuous with the smooth ER and with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: rER consists of interconnected, flattened, parallel cisternae whose outer surface is studded with ribosomes.
explanations.C: Correct. Ribosome-associated basophilia caused by rough ER is localised or focal (patchy, concentrated where the rER is), not diffuse; diffuse basophilia scattered evenly through the cytosol is instead caused by free ribosomes, not by rER. Rough ER and free ribosomes both make cytoplasm basophilic, but the pattern each produces is different, and this question tests that distinction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: rER-synthesised protein is packaged into transfer vesicles for delivery to the Golgi apparatus.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish rER-associated (localised/focal) basophilia from the diffuse basophilia caused by free ribosomes.

questions.title: Main organelle for protein synthesis
questions.question: The main organelle responsible for protein synthesis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The smooth ER, by definition, lacks the ribosomes needed for protein synthesis.
explanations.B: Correct. The rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with ribosomes on its outer, cytoplasmic surface. Those ribosomes translate mRNA into protein and feed the growing chain directly into the rER lumen. This ribosome-rich structure makes the rough ER the organelle chiefly responsible for synthesising protein destined for secretion, the plasma membrane, or the lysosome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proteasomes degrade protein; they do not synthesise it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages protein after synthesis; it does not synthesise it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endosomes are sorting compartments in the endocytic pathway; they play no role in protein synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the rough ER, via its attached ribosomes, is the main site of protein synthesis for export.

questions.title: Statement not true of the Golgi complex
questions.question: About Golgi complex, all are true except:

options.A: Its saccules are interconnected through transfer vesicles.
options.D: So numerous in steroid forming cells.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: Golgi saccules exchange material via transfer vesicles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: silver impregnation demonstrates the Golgi apparatus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: the Golgi distributes and sorts membrane proteins to their correct destinations.
explanations.D: Correct. A prominent, numerous Golgi apparatus is a feature of cells secreting a bulky glycoprotein product, not of steroid-forming cells; steroid-forming cells instead are characterised by abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum, since their small lipid-soluble hormone product needs little further Golgi packaging. Attaching Golgi prominence to steroid cells swaps the organelle emphasis that actually defines that cell type.

questions.learning_objective: State that Golgi prominence marks a bulky-glycoprotein-secreting cell, not a steroid-forming cell (which is instead sER-rich).

questions.title: Cells showing a Golgi negative image
questions.question: Golgi apparatus may appear as -ve Golgi image in:

options.C: (plasma cell & osteoblast) Highly protein secreting cells.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Steroid-forming cells have a comparatively small Golgi and a strongly acidophilic (not basophilic) cytoplasm dominated by sER, so the pale-Golgi-against-basophilic-background contrast is not their classic feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Protein secreting cells" in general is too broad; the negative Golgi image is most classically and specifically associated with the highly protein-secreting cells named in option C.
explanations.C: Correct. The negative Golgi image is a pale, unstained area beside the nucleus, seen where the Golgi apparatus interrupts the otherwise strongly basophilic (rER-rich) cytoplasm of a highly protein-secreting cell in a routine H&E section; the plasma cell is the textbook example, and the osteoblast (secreting large amounts of collagen for bone matrix) shows the same pattern. This is the classic worked example the question is built around.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dividing cells are not the cell type this Golgi feature is classically associated with.

questions.learning_objective: Name the plasma cell and the osteoblast as the classic examples showing a negative Golgi image in H&E.

questions.title: True statement about Golgi saccules
questions.question: One of the following is true about Golgi Saccules:

options.A: Their mature faces receive the transfer vesicles.
options.B: Their convex surfaces give rise to secretory vesicles.
options.C: They are prominent in steroid secreting cells
options.D: They are prominent in protein secreting cells
options.E: They are continuous with the nuclear membrane.

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the immature (cis, entry) face, not the mature face, that receives transfer vesicles from the rER.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secretory vesicles bud from the concave, trans (exit/maturing) face, not the convex (cis) face.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Steroid-secreting cells are characterised by abundant smooth ER, not by a prominent Golgi apparatus.
explanations.D: Correct. Protein-secreting cells route their newly synthesised export protein through the Golgi for glycosylation, sorting and packaging. This heavy traffic keeps their Golgi saccules correspondingly well developed and prominent. Golgi prominence, alongside a rich rough ER, is therefore a marker of a cell dedicated to protein secretion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the rough ER's outer membrane, not the Golgi saccules, that is continuous with the nuclear envelope.

questions.learning_objective: State that Golgi saccules are prominent in protein-secreting cells and identify the entry/exit-face orientation of vesicle traffic.

questions.title: Statement not true of the Golgi apparatus
questions.question: About Golgi apparatus, all are true except:

options.A: Seen as -ve Golgi image in Plasma cell & Osteoblast.
options.C: In polar secretory cells it is located supranuclear.
options.D: In nonpolar secretory cells is located perinuclear (circumnuclear).

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the plasma cell and osteoblast are the classic examples of the negative Golgi image.
explanations.B: Correct. The Golgi apparatus is not demonstrated by routine haematoxylin and eosin staining; H&E shows it only indirectly, as a pale negative image against basophilic cytoplasm. Positive demonstration of the Golgi itself requires a special stain such as silver or osmium, not H&E. Claiming H&E stains the Golgi directly is the error being tested.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: in a polar secretory cell discharging at one free surface, the Golgi lies supranuclear, between the nucleus and the secretory surface.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: in a nonpolar cell such as a neuron, with no single secretory face, the Golgi lies perinuclear.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Golgi is not directly demonstrated by H&E and recall its supranuclear/perinuclear positioning rule.

questions.title: Function not carried out by the Golgi
questions.question: All following are functions of Golgi except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: sorting protein to its correct destination is a core Golgi function.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: completing and modifying carbohydrate side chains (glycosylation) is a core Golgi function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: processing prohormones and proproteins into their mature, active form is a core Golgi function.
explanations.D: Correct. Glycogenesis (glycogen synthesis) is carried out by soluble cytosolic enzymes such as glycogen synthase and branching enzyme; it is not one of the Golgi's packaging/processing functions. The Golgi's role with carbohydrate is limited to modifying the sugar chains already attached to secretory glycoproteins (glycosylation), which is a different process from building the glycogen storage polymer from scratch.

questions.learning_objective: List the Golgi's true functions (sorting, glycosylation, prohormone/protein modification) and exclude glycogenesis.

questions.title: Feature of the regulated secretory pathway
questions.question: In regulated secretory pathway:

options.A: Secretory vesicles are instantly released by exocytosis
options.B: Secretory vesicles are stored & concentrated then released on demand
options.C: Secretory products are released by diffusion
options.D: Secretory proteins are recycled & digested by lysosomes.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Instant release with no storage step describes the constitutive pathway, not the regulated one.
explanations.B: Correct. In the regulated secretory pathway, the product is packaged into secretory vesicles that are stored and concentrated in the cytoplasm and released only when a specific trigger arrives — for example, an islet beta cell holding insulin granules until a rise in blood glucose signals release. This store-then-release-on-demand pattern is the defining feature of the regulated pathway, distinguishing it from the constitutive pathway's continuous release.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Regulated secretion is by vesicle exocytosis on trigger, not by passive diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes lysosomal digestion/turnover, not the export of a normal secretory product by the regulated pathway.

questions.learning_objective: Define the regulated secretory pathway as storing product for signal-triggered release.

questions.title: Feature of the constitutive secretory pathway
questions.question: In constitutive secretory pathway:

options.A: Secretory vesicles are instantly released by exocytosis
options.B: Secretory vesicles are stored & concentrated then released on demand
options.C: Secretory products are released by diffusion
options.D: Secretory proteins are recycled & digested by lysosomes.

explanations.A: Correct. In the constitutive secretory pathway there is no storage step at all: vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release their contents by exocytosis continuously and immediately as they are made, the pattern seen in a fibroblast or osteoblast exporting procollagen for connective tissue and bone. This instant, unregulated release is what distinguishes the constitutive pathway from the store-and-trigger regulated pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Storage and demand-triggered release describes the regulated pathway, not the constitutive one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Constitutive secretion is by vesicle exocytosis, not by passive diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes lysosomal digestion/turnover, not the constitutive export of a normal secretory product.

questions.learning_objective: Define the constitutive secretory pathway as continuous, immediate exocytosis with no storage step.

questions.title: Most acidic compartment
questions.question: Which of the following is more acidic:

explanations.A: Correct. Along the endocytic/digestive pathway, pH falls progressively as material moves onward: a phagosome starts near-neutral, the early endosome is only mildly acidic (about pH 6-6.5), and the late endosome is more acidic still (about pH 5-6). Fusion of a primary lysosome with the substrate then creates the secondary lysosome, the most acidic compartment of the whole sequence, around pH 4.5-5. This is the pH level needed for maximal activity of its hydrolytic enzymes, which is why the secondary lysosome, not an earlier compartment, is the most acidic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A phagosome, freshly formed from plasma membrane, starts close to neutral pH and has not yet undergone the acidification that follows in the endosome/lysosome pathway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The early endosome is only mildly acidic, less acidic than the late endosome and far less acidic than the secondary lysosome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The late endosome is more acidic than the early endosome but still less acidic than the fully activated secondary lysosome.

questions.learning_objective: Rank the endocytic/digestive compartments (phagosome, early endosome, late endosome, secondary lysosome) from least to most acidic.

questions.title: Process by which the cell engulfs extracellular fluid
questions.question: PROCESS BY WHICH THE CELL ENGULFS EXTRACELLULAR FLUID:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis engulfs solid particles ("cell eating"), not fluid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exocytosis is the reverse process, releasing material out of the cell, not taking fluid in.
explanations.C: Correct. Pinocytosis ("cell drinking") is the bulk uptake of extracellular fluid and whatever is dissolved in it. Small invaginations of the plasma membrane pinch off inward as fluid-filled vesicles to carry this out. Unlike receptor-mediated endocytosis, pinocytosis needs no specific receptor protein to occur.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Receptor-mediated endocytosis takes in a specific ligand bound to its receptor, not extracellular fluid in bulk.

questions.learning_objective: Define pinocytosis as the bulk uptake of extracellular fluid.

questions.title: Endocytosis of particulate matter
questions.question: Endocytosis of particulate matter:

explanations.A: Correct. Phagocytosis ("cell eating") is the process by which a cell surrounds a solid particle, such as a bacterium, with pseudopodia. The particle is then engulfed into a membrane-bound phagosome. This pathway is specifically for particulate (solid) material, in contrast with pinocytosis, which takes in dissolved fluid instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exocytosis releases material out of the cell; it is not a form of endocytosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pinocytosis takes in fluid, not solid particulate matter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Receptor-mediated endocytosis takes in a specific soluble ligand bound to its receptor, not solid particulate matter.

questions.learning_objective: Define phagocytosis as the endocytosis of solid particulate matter.

questions.title: Process by which materials are extruded from the cell
questions.question: Materials are extruded out of the cell by a process known as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis takes solid material into the cell; it does not extrude material out.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pinocytosis takes fluid into the cell; it does not extrude material out.
explanations.C: Correct. Exocytosis is the process by which a cytoplasmic vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and discharges its contents to the outside. The membrane's continuity is preserved throughout, since the vesicle membrane simply becomes part of the plasma membrane. This is how a merocrine gland secretes its product, and it is the direct reverse of endocytosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis and receptor-mediated endocytosis together) takes material into the cell; it does not extrude material out.

questions.learning_objective: Define exocytosis as the vesicle-mediated extrusion of material from the cell.

questions.title: Protein coating coated vesicles
questions.question: Coated vesicles are coated by cytoplasmic protein called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Extrinsic protein" is a general term for a peripheral membrane protein, not the specific vesicle-coat protein being asked for.
explanations.B: Correct. Clathrin is the cytoplasmic-surface coat protein that assembles over a patch of membrane during receptor-mediated endocytosis. This assembly forms a coated pit, which then pinches off inward as a coated vesicle. The clathrin coat is what gives this type of vesicle its name and is later shed once the vesicle has formed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tubulin is the protein subunit of microtubules, unrelated to vesicle coating.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dynein is a microtubule motor protein (powering ciliary beating and retrograde transport), not a vesicle-coat protein.

questions.learning_objective: Name clathrin as the coat protein of a receptor-mediated-endocytosis coated vesicle.

questions.title: Statement not true of lysosomes
questions.question: About lysosome the following is true except:

options.A: Its membrane is formed of unique type of phospholipids
options.B: are Heterogenous vesicles (of variable density) & more acidic
options.C: Stained with histochemical stain for catalase enzymes

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the lysosomal membrane has an unusual phospholipid composition that helps protect it from its own enzymes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: lysosomes are heterogeneous in density (varying with digestive stage) and are markedly acidic compared with the cytosol.
explanations.C: Correct. The catalase histochemical reaction is the marker stain for the peroxisome, not the lysosome; the lysosome's own histochemical marker is the acid phosphatase reaction. Assigning the catalase stain to the lysosome confuses it with the other small membranous, enzyme-rich organelle it is most often paired with in exam questions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: lysosomes are rich in acid hydrolase enzymes such as acid phosphatase, protease and nuclease.

questions.learning_objective: State that the catalase histochemical stain marks the peroxisome, not the lysosome, whose own marker is acid phosphatase.

questions.title: Stain used to demonstrate lysosomes
questions.question: Lysosomes are stained by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Iron haematoxylin is the classic mitochondrial stain, not the lysosomal one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Silver stain classically demonstrates the Golgi apparatus, not the lysosome.
explanations.C: Correct. Acid phosphatase is a hydrolytic enzyme concentrated in the lysosome. A histochemical reaction that localises acid phosphatase activity is therefore the standard method for identifying lysosomes. Lysosomes cannot otherwise be distinguished from other small cytoplasmic vesicles by routine light-microscopic staining, which is why this enzyme-specific reaction is needed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PAS demonstrates carbohydrate-rich structures such as glycogen, the basement membrane and the cell coat, not the lysosome specifically.

questions.learning_objective: Name the acid phosphatase histochemical reaction as the standard method for demonstrating lysosomes.

questions.title: Vesicle whose membrane is not derived from the plasma membrane
questions.question: One of the following is not surrounded by a membrane part of the cell membrane:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A phagosome forms by inward pinching-off of a patch of plasma membrane during phagocytosis, so its membrane is plasma-membrane-derived.
explanations.B: Correct. A secretory vesicle buds from the trans face of the Golgi apparatus, carrying newly packaged secretory product; its membrane originates from the Golgi, not from the plasma membrane, even though it later fuses with and becomes part of the plasma membrane at the moment of exocytosis. This makes it the one vesicle type among the options whose membrane is not, at origin, a part of the cell membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pinocytic vesicle forms by inward pinching-off of a patch of plasma membrane during pinocytosis, so its membrane is plasma-membrane-derived.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A coated (receptor-mediated endocytosis) vesicle forms by inward pinching-off of a clathrin-coated patch of plasma membrane, so its membrane is plasma-membrane-derived.

questions.learning_objective: Classify cytoplasmic vesicles by membrane origin: secretory vesicles from the Golgi versus endocytic vesicles from the plasma membrane.

questions.title: Statement not true of coated vesicles
questions.question: About coated vesicles, all are true except:

options.A: Formed through receptor mediated endocytosis [e.g. hormones & lipoproteins].
options.B: Fuse with lysosome to form autophagosome.
options.C: Its cytoplasmic surface is coated with Clathrin protein.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: coated vesicles form via receptor-mediated endocytosis of ligands such as hormones and lipoproteins.
explanations.B: Correct. A coated vesicle fuses with an endosome, not with a lysosome, and its cargo does not form an autophagosome; an autophagosome instead forms when a primary lysosome (or autophagic vacuole) engulfs the cell's own worn-out organelles, an entirely different process from receptor-mediated endocytosis of extracellular material. Attaching "forms an autophagosome" to the coated-vesicle/lysosome fusion step mixes up endocytic cargo handling with autophagy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: the cytoplasmic surface of a coated vesicle is coated with clathrin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: a coated vesicle fuses with an endosome as the next step of its trafficking.

questions.learning_objective: State that a coated vesicle fuses with an endosome, not a lysosome, and that autophagosome formation is a separate (autophagy) process.

questions.title: Statement not true of peroxisomes
questions.question: Peroxisomes or microbodies, the following is true except:

options.A: Present near sER & may have electron dense core granule
options.B: Contain oxidative enzymes to degrade drugs & alcohol
options.D: Contain enzymes for B oxidation of fatty acids

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: peroxisomes are often found near the sER and can show an electron-dense core (nucleoid) on EM.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: peroxisomal oxidases degrade drugs and alcohol, generating hydrogen peroxide that peroxisomal catalase then breaks down.
explanations.C: Correct. Acid hydrolases are the defining enzyme content of the lysosome, not the peroxisome; the peroxisome instead contains oxidases (which generate hydrogen peroxide) and catalase (which destroys it), together with beta-oxidation enzymes. This question has no printed answer letter anywhere on the source page and is keyed editorially from standard cell-biology knowledge: acid hydrolases belong to the lysosome, so "contains acid hydrolases" is the false statement about the peroxisome that the "except" stem is looking for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: peroxisomes contain the enzymes for beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids.

questions.learning_objective: State that acid hydrolases are a lysosomal, not peroxisomal, enzyme content, distinguishing the two small membranous organelles.

questions.title: Origin of lipofuscin pigment
questions.question: Lipofuscine pigment result from:

options.B: Accumulated residual bodies in long lived cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Residual bodies can be exocytosed, but the lipofuscin pigment specifically results from residual bodies that are retained, not expelled.
explanations.B: Correct. When a secondary lysosome finishes digesting its substrate, the undigested residue left behind is a residual body; in long-lived, non-dividing cells such as cardiac muscle and nerve cells, these residual bodies are not cleared but accumulate over the years as the age pigment lipofuscin, a membrane-bound remnant of repeated lysosomal digestion. This accumulation-with-age pattern is why lipofuscin is used as a marker of cellular ageing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pinocytosis is a route of material entry into the cell, not the origin of the lipofuscin pigment itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lipofuscin is a pigment derived from a residual body, not an endosome, which is an earlier, distinct stage of the endocytic pathway.

questions.learning_objective: State that lipofuscin is the accumulated residual-body pigment of long-lived, non-dividing cells.

questions.title: Statement not true of diffuse basophilia
questions.question: About Diffuse basophilia, all are true except:

options.D: Found in cells actively forming cytoplasmic proteins.

explanations.A: Correct. Steroid-forming cells are typically acidophilic, not basophilic, because they are dominated by smooth endoplasmic reticulum (which has no ribosomes) rather than by free ribosomes or rough ER; diffuse basophilia, by contrast, is produced by free ribosomes scattered through the cytosol. Attributing diffuse basophilia to a steroid-forming cell reverses the staining pattern that actually distinguishes a steroidogenic cell from a ribosome-rich, protein-forming one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: dividing cells, which are actively synthesising protein for growth and division, show diffuse basophilia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: diffuse (as opposed to localised/focal) basophilia is caused specifically by free ribosomes scattered through the cytosol.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: cells actively forming cytoplasmic (non-exported) protein rely on free ribosomes and so show diffuse basophilia.

questions.learning_objective: State that diffuse basophilia (from free ribosomes) is not a feature of the sER-rich, acidophilic steroid-forming cell.

questions.title: Site of ribosomal RNA synthesis
questions.question: Ribosomal RNA is synthesized (transcripted) by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The smooth ER has no role in RNA transcription.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The rough ER translates mRNA into protein; it does not transcribe rRNA.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus processes protein after synthesis; it plays no role in RNA transcription.
explanations.D: Correct. The nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA gene transcription: its pars amorpha (nucleolar organiser) carries the rDNA, its pars fibrosa contains the newly transcribed rRNA, and its pars granulosa contains the maturing ribosomal subunits before they pass through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm. This transcription-and-assembly role is the defining function of the nucleolus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA transcription and ribosomal subunit assembly.

questions.title: Component not part of the cytoskeleton
questions.question: Cytoskeleton of the cell is formed of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microtubules are one of the three recognised cytoskeletal filament systems.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intermediate filaments are one of the three recognised cytoskeletal filament systems.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Microfilaments (thin, actin filaments) are one of the three recognised cytoskeletal filament systems.
explanations.D: Correct. The general cell cytoskeleton is defined as three filament systems only: microtubules, microfilaments (actin) and intermediate filaments. Thick (myosin) filaments are part of the specialised contractile apparatus of muscle, working together with thin actin filaments, but they are not counted as a fourth component of the cytoskeleton itself.

questions.learning_objective: List the three cytoskeletal filament systems and exclude myosin thick filaments.

questions.title: Statement not true of intermediate filaments
questions.question: About intermediate filaments the following is true except:

options.A: Heterogenous group of filaments with variable protein structure
options.B: Polar filaments with plus & minus ends
options.C: Help to ensure equal distribution of the tensile forces throughout the cells e.g. in smooth muscles and keratinocytes of skin.
options.D: Detection of type of intermediate filament in tumor cells help to know the origin of the tumor

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: intermediate filaments are a heterogeneous group, with a different protein composition in different tissues.
explanations.B: Correct. Intermediate filaments are non-polar structures, with no distinct plus and minus ends; polarity with defined plus/minus ends is instead a feature of microtubules and actin microfilaments. Assigning plus/minus polarity to intermediate filaments confuses them with the other two, polar cytoskeletal systems.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: intermediate filaments distribute tensile (mechanical stress) forces evenly through the cell, a role illustrated in smooth muscle and skin keratinocytes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: because each tissue's intermediate filament protein is distinctive, identifying it in a tumour helps establish the tumour's tissue of origin.

questions.learning_objective: State that intermediate filaments are non-polar, unlike microtubules and microfilaments.

questions.title: Statement not true of microfilaments (actin filaments)
questions.question: Microfilaments [actin filaments] the following is true except:

options.A: present as a network under cell membrane of most cells (cell cortex) & core of Microvili.
options.B: in cells other than muscle cells, they are dynamic unstable structure
options.C: formed of globular subunits, called G - actin.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: microfilaments form the cortical network beneath the plasma membrane and the structural core of microvilli.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: outside of stable muscle contractile arrangements, actin filaments are dynamic and readily assembled/disassembled.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: microfilaments are polymers of globular G-actin subunits.
explanations.D: Correct. A microfilament (thin/actin filament) is 5-7 nm in diameter, not 10 nm; 10 nm is instead the diameter figure associated with intermediate filaments. Mixing up the diameter figures of the different cytoskeletal filament classes is the error this question tests.

questions.learning_objective: State the microfilament diameter (5-7 nm) and distinguish it from the intermediate filament's 10 nm.

questions.title: Statement not true of intermediate filaments
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning intermediate filaments is true EXCEPT;

options.C: they are stable non polarized structure.
options.D: present in the nucleus and cytoplasm.

explanations.A: Correct. Dynein is a microtubule-associated motor protein, not an intermediate-filament protein; intermediate filaments are instead built from a tissue-specific structural protein such as keratin, desmin, vimentin, GFAP or a neurofilament protein, and nuclear lamins in the case of the nuclear envelope. Assigning dynein to intermediate filaments confuses a motor protein of a different cytoskeletal system with the structural proteins that actually form intermediate filaments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: providing structural, tensile support is the core role of intermediate filaments.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: intermediate filaments are stable and non-polarised, unlike the dynamic, polar microtubules and microfilaments.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: intermediate filaments occur both in the cytoplasm (keratin, vimentin etc.) and in the nucleus (lamins of the nuclear lamina).

questions.learning_objective: State that intermediate filaments are built of tissue-specific structural proteins (not dynein) and exist in both cytoplasm and nucleus.

questions.title: Statement not true of actin filaments
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning actin filaments is true EXCEPT;

options.C: form network in the periphery of cell called cell cortex.

explanations.A: Correct. The mitotic spindle is built of microtubules, not actin filaments; actin filaments instead form the contractile ring that pinches the dividing cell in two at the cleavage furrow, a separate structure from the spindle. Assigning spindle formation to actin confuses it with the microtubule cytoskeleton.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: actin filaments are polymers of globular G-actin subunits.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: actin filaments form the cortical network at the cell periphery, the cell cortex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: actin (thin) filaments are about 7 nm in diameter.

questions.learning_objective: State that the mitotic spindle is built of microtubules, not actin filaments.

questions.title: Statement not true of microtubules
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning microtubules is true EXCEPT;

options.B: move the vesicles inside the cytoplasm.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: microtubules are built from alpha- and beta-tubulin dimers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: motor proteins moving along microtubules transport vesicles and organelles through the cytoplasm.
explanations.C: Correct. Microtubules are dynamic, not stable, structures — they continually lengthen and shorten by adding or losing tubulin at their ends — and they are polar, with a distinct plus and minus end, not non-polarised. This directly contradicts intermediate filaments, which really are stable and non-polar, and swapping the two filament systems' properties is the error being tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: microtubules are approximately 24-25 nm in diameter.

questions.learning_objective: State that microtubules are dynamic and polar, not stable/non-polarised (a property of intermediate filaments instead).

questions.title: Use of a substance that stops microtubule formation
questions.question: Substance stopping microtubule formation (e.g. colchicines) can be used for:

options.C: Treatment of malignant tumors e.g. cancer.

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. This is true (blocking microtubule assembly stops the mitotic spindle from forming, arresting mitosis) but it is not the only correct use among the options.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. This is true (arresting cells in metaphase with intact, condensed chromosomes is how a colchicine-type agent is used to prepare a karyotype) but it is not the only correct use among the options.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. This is true (anti-microtubule chemotherapy drugs arrest the mitotic spindle of rapidly dividing cancer cells) but it is not the only correct use among the options.
explanations.D: Correct. The mitotic spindle is built of microtubules, so a substance such as colchicine that prevents microtubule assembly blocks spindle formation and arrests cell division at metaphase. This single mechanism underlies all three uses listed. It stops mitosis experimentally, it arrests cells in metaphase with intact chromosomes to prepare a karyotype, and it kills rapidly dividing cancer cells therapeutically.

questions.learning_objective: Connect microtubule-formation blockade (colchicine) to mitotic arrest and its uses in karyotyping and cancer chemotherapy.

questions.title: Site of microtubule assembly and disassembly
questions.question: Assembly and disassembly of microtubules occurs in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes synthesise protein; they play no role in microtubule assembly.
explanations.B: Correct. The centrosome is the cell's microtubule organising centre (MTOC), containing a pair of centrioles surrounded by a tubulin-rich matrix. It directs the nucleation, growth (assembly) and shrinkage (disassembly) of microtubules. Each microtubule's minus end is anchored at the centrosome while its plus end extends outward into the cytoplasm, which is why assembly and disassembly are centred there.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The nucleus houses the genome; it is not the site of microtubule assembly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosomal subunits; it plays no role in microtubule assembly.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Peroxisomes handle oxidative reactions; they play no role in microtubule assembly.

questions.learning_objective: State that the centrosome (MTOC) directs microtubule assembly and disassembly.

questions.title: Structure that is not an MTOC
questions.question: MTOCs (microtubules organization centers) include the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the centriole (as part of the centrosome) is a microtubule organising centre.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: the basal body, structurally identical to a centriole, organises the microtubules of the ciliary/flagellar axoneme, making it an MTOC.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: the centromere/kinetochore nucleates the kinetochore microtubules of the mitotic spindle, making it an MTOC.
explanations.D: Correct. The mitochondrion is the site of ATP production, not a site of microtubule nucleation. It has no tubulin-organising matrix of its own and plays no role in directing microtubule assembly. It is therefore not an MTOC, unlike the centriole, basal body and centromere/kinetochore, which all genuinely nucleate microtubules.

questions.learning_objective: List the true microtubule organising centres (centriole, basal body, centromere/kinetochore) and exclude the mitochondrion.

questions.title: Statement not true of centrioles
questions.question: About Centrioles, all true except:

options.B: Formed of 9 doublets & 2 singlets of microtubules.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: a centriole's wall is nine triplets of microtubules (27 microtubules), with no central pair.
explanations.B: Correct. The 9 doublets plus 2 central singlets (9+2) arrangement describes the axoneme of a cilium or flagellum, not a centriole; a centriole has 9 triplets and no central microtubules at all (9+0). Confusing the centriole's 9+0 triplet structure with the cilium's 9+2 doublet-and-singlet axoneme is the error this question is built to catch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: centrioles (as the centrosome) are typically located near the Golgi apparatus, close to the nucleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: centrioles are demonstrated by iron haematoxylin staining.

questions.learning_objective: State that the centriole is built of 9 microtubule triplets (9+0), not the cilium's 9 doublets plus 2 singlets (9+2).

questions.title: Structure of the ciliary shaft
questions.question: The shaft of cilia:

options.A: Is not covered by cell membrane.
options.C: Identical to the basal body structure.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ciliary shaft is covered by cell membrane, a direct continuation of the plasma membrane.
explanations.B: Correct. The ciliary shaft's internal skeleton, the axoneme, has the 9+2 arrangement: nine peripheral microtubule doublets (18 microtubules) surrounding two central single microtubules, giving 20 microtubules in all. This is one microtubule-pair fewer than the centriole/basal body's 9 triplets (27 microtubules), because the central singlet pair is unique to the motile axoneme and is not present in the centriole.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The shaft's axoneme (9+2, with a central pair) is not identical to the basal body's structure (9 triplets, 9+0, no central pair); it is the basal body, not the shaft, that has the same structure as a centriole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ciliary beating is coordinated and directional, not irregular; this directional beat is what allows cilia to move fluid or mucus in one consistent direction across an epithelial surface.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ciliary shaft's axoneme is built of microtubules, not actin filaments.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the ciliary shaft's 9+2, 20-microtubule axoneme and its membrane covering, distinguishing it from the basal body's 9+0 triplet structure.

questions.title: Structure that powers ciliary movement
questions.question: Movement of cilia depend on:

explanations.A: Correct. Dynein arms are ATPase motor proteins attached along each peripheral microtubule doublet of the ciliary axoneme. Using energy from ATP hydrolysis, they cause adjacent doublets to slide against one another. Because the doublets are cross-linked rather than free to slide indefinitely, this sliding is converted into the coordinated bending wave that is seen as the ciliary beat.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Kinesin is a microtubule motor protein used mainly for anterograde intracellular transport, not for powering the ciliary beat.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myosin is the actin-based motor protein of muscle contraction (and some cytoplasmic transport), not the motor of the microtubule-based ciliary axoneme.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Actin is not a structural component of the ciliary axoneme, which is built of microtubules, not actin filaments.

questions.learning_objective: State that dynein arms, sliding along the axonemal microtubule doublets, power the ciliary beat.

questions.title: Statement not true of the proteasome
questions.question: About proteasome, all true except:

options.B: degrades misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm
options.C: formed of protein rings & guiding molecules

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the proteasome is a non-membranous organelle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: the proteasome degrades misfolded and abnormal proteins in the cytosol.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: the proteasome is a barrel-shaped assembly of protein rings together with regulatory/guiding cap molecules that recognise ubiquitin-tagged substrates.
explanations.D: Correct. The proteasome is specifically a non-membranous organelle, built entirely of protein rings and regulatory subunits without any limiting membrane. Calling it "membranous" directly contradicts option A's true statement and is the deliberate self-contradiction this stem is built around. This distinguishes the proteasome from membranous protein-degrading organelles such as the lysosome, which does have a limiting membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that the proteasome is non-membranous, distinguishing it from membranous organelles such as the lysosome.

questions.title: Cellular component that is not a polar structure
questions.question: All of the following cellular components are polar structures except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: the Golgi apparatus is a polarised structure, with a distinct entry (cis) face and exit (trans) face.
explanations.B: Correct. Intermediate filaments are the one cytoskeletal system that is non-polar, with no distinguishable ends and no directional assembly; polarity, with defined plus and minus ends (or, for the Golgi, cis and trans faces), is instead a shared feature of the Golgi apparatus, microfilaments and microtubules. This lack of polarity is what sets intermediate filaments apart from the other structures listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: actin microfilaments are polar, with a distinct plus (barbed) and minus (pointed) end.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is true: microtubules are polar, with a distinct plus and minus end.

questions.learning_objective: State that intermediate filaments are the non-polar exception among cytoskeletal/organelle structures otherwise built with directional polarity.

questions.title: Statement not true of glycogen inclusions
questions.question: About glycogen inclusions, one is not true:

options.A: stained purple with PAS and red with Best's carmine
options.B: Alpha particles: rosette shaped present in liver cells
options.D: Present as membrane bound granules in the cytoplasm

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is true: glycogen stains purple/magenta with PAS and red with Best's carmine, both carbohydrate-selective stains.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is true: alpha particles are rosette-shaped clusters of glycogen granules, characteristic of hepatocytes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is true: beta particles are the smaller, discrete single-granule form typical of skeletal muscle and most other cells.
explanations.D: Correct. Glycogen is a free, non-membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion; unlike lipofuscin, which really is membrane-bound because it is the residue of a lysosome (a residual body), glycogen particles are simply granules of stored polysaccharide sitting directly in the cytosol with no membrane around them. Calling glycogen membrane-bound is the false statement being tested.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish glycogen alpha (liver, rosette) and beta (discrete) particles, and state that glycogen, unlike lipofuscin, is not membrane-bound.

questions.title: Most numerous endogenous pigment
questions.question: Most numerous endogenous pigment is:

explanations.A: Correct. Haemoglobin is packed into every one of the body's roughly 25 trillion circulating red blood cells. Counted molecule for molecule across that enormous cell population, it is by sheer bulk the most numerous endogenous pigment in the body. It far exceeds melanin, which is confined to melanocytes and other pigmented cells, and lipofuscin, which is confined to long-lived, non-dividing cells such as neurons and cardiac myocytes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Melanin is an endogenous pigment, but it is restricted to melanocytes and pigment-containing cells, a much smaller population than the red-cell mass carrying haemoglobin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipofuscin is an endogenous pigment, but it accumulates only in long-lived, non-dividing cells such as cardiac muscle and neurons, a small fraction of total body cells compared with circulating red cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carotene is an exogenous (dietary), not endogenous, pigment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify haemoglobin as the most numerous endogenous pigment and carotene as exogenous, not endogenous.

questions.title: The one membrane-bound inclusion
questions.question: The only inclusion which is membrane bound:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipid droplets are free in the cytosol, with no limiting membrane of their own.
explanations.B: Correct. Lipofuscin is the accumulated, undigested residue of a lysosome's own single membrane — a residual body that persists in a long-lived cell — so, unlike the body's other cytoplasmic inclusions, it retains a membrane around it. This lysosomal ancestry is exactly what makes lipofuscin the one membrane-bound inclusion among the options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glycogen particles (alpha and beta) are free granules in the cytosol, with no membrane around them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myoglobin is a soluble, non-membrane-bound oxygen-storage protein dissolved in the sarcoplasm of muscle cells, not a membrane-bound inclusion.

questions.learning_objective: State that lipofuscin, as a lysosomal residual body, is the one membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion.
